summary: Jesus crosses the Kidron to a familiar garden, where Judas arrives with soldiers and officers. Jesus identifies himself, protects the disciples, rejects Peter's sword, and accepts the Father's cup. Interrogated by Annas and transferred to Caiaphas, he is denied three times by Peter beside a charcoal fire. Before Pilate, Jesus describes a kingdom not sourced from this world and a vocation to testify to truth; Pilate answers with a question and releases Barabbas instead.
whyItMatters: John's passion begins with Jesus neither surprised nor powerless. His self-giving protects others and rejects violent defense, while Peter's courage collapses beside an ordinary fire. Before empire, Jesus's kingdom is not sustained by the world's mechanisms, yet it publicly challenges false judgment through truth.

context.author: The anonymous Fourth Gospel narrator, presenting arrest and trials through sovereignty, testimony, irony, and interwoven scenes
context.audience: Readers needing Roman and high-priestly procedure, Passover purity, and John's context-sensitive group labels
context.date: The night and morning before crucifixion during Passover preparations
context.setting: A garden across the Kidron, high-priestly courtyards, and Pilate's Jerusalem headquarters
context.literaryForm: Passion narrative alternating Jesus's faithful testimony with Peter's denial, then a dramatic royal trial

outline.heading: Jesus is arrested in the garden and protects his disciples
Annas questions Jesus while Peter denies him
Pilate questions Jesus about kingship and truth

keyVerses.text: They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus said to them, “I am he.” Judas also, who betrayed him, was standing with them.
keyVerses.why: Jesus steps forward and identifies himself while the arresting force recoils.

keyVerses.text: Jesus answered, “My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, then my servants would fight, that I wouldn’t be delivered to the Jews. But now my Kingdom is not from here.”
keyVerses.why: The kingdom's source is not the world's violent order, as its servants' nonviolence demonstrates.

keyVerses.text: Pilate therefore said to him, “Are you a king then?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”
keyVerses.why: Jesus defines royal vocation through witness to truth rather than coercive self-preservation.

questions.question: Why does John say ‘garden’ rather than Gethsemane?
questions.answer: John names the Kidron crossing and a garden familiar to Jesus and the disciples but never calls it Gethsemane or narrates the Synoptic agony prayer. Each Gospel shapes remembered events with distinctive emphases. John foregrounds Jesus knowing what will happen, stepping forward, protecting the disciples, and willingly taking the cup.

questions.question: Who comes to arrest Jesus?
questions.answer: A speira can denote a Roman cohort or a detachment from one, while officers come from the chief priests and Pharisees. The size is uncertain, so the full technical number should not be assumed. John's mixed force shows both Roman and Jerusalem-authority involvement before the narrative assigns decisions and actions more precisely.

questions.question: Why do they draw back when Jesus says ‘I am he’?
questions.answer: Egō eimi answers their search for Jesus of Nazareth and naturally means ‘I am he.’ Yet the repeated formula, Jesus's initiative, and the armed group's falling backward give the identification theophanic resonance. John presents arrest as occurring only after Jesus openly gives himself and secures his disciples' release.

questions.question: What does Jesus's rejection of Peter's sword establish?
questions.answer: Peter's strike resembles the world's way of preserving leaders through violence. Jesus stops it and speaks of the cup the Father has given, interpreting arrest as obedient mission rather than military defeat. Verse 36 later makes the same logic political: if his kingdom originated from this world, his servants would fight—but they do not.

questions.question: Why is Jesus questioned by Annas if Caiaphas is high priest?
questions.answer: Annas had been high priest and remained the powerful patriarch of the high-priestly family; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office that year. John narrates an informal interrogation before Annas and then transfer to Caiaphas. The scene's procedural irregularity sharpens Jesus's appeal to public teaching and lawful witnesses.

questions.question: What does the charcoal fire contribute to Peter's denial?
questions.answer: Anthrakia is a charcoal fire, a rare word that appears again at Peter's restoration in chapter 21. Here it supplies warmth, light, smell, and a circle of witnesses while Peter repeatedly denies belonging to Jesus. The later breakfast scene does not erase this failure; it deliberately returns Peter to a sensory setting where love and vocation can be addressed.

questions.question: Who are ‘the Jews’ in the Roman trial scenes?
questions.answer: Here Ioudaioi most often denotes the Jerusalem delegation or authorities interacting with Pilate, not Jewish people universally. Jesus, Peter, the beloved disciple, and all the priestly figures are Jewish, while Rome holds execution power. Responsible reading names each actor and resists later Christian attempts to transfer collective guilt across generations.

questions.question: Does ‘not of this world’ mean Jesus's kingdom is apolitical?
questions.answer: The Greek ek means ‘from’ or ‘out of’: this world's order is not the kingdom's source. Jesus explains the difference by the absence of violent fighting, not by saying his rule has no public consequences. His truth confronts priestly expediency and Roman judgment, while rejecting their means of domination.

questions.question: What is the irony of Barabbas?
questions.answer: Pilate offers a Passover release while publicly declaring he finds no case against Jesus. The crowd chooses Barabbas, described as a lēstēs—a bandit or insurrectionist, not merely a petty thief. The nonviolent king is exchanged for a figure associated with violent resistance, exposing the political alternatives surrounding the cross.

glossary.def: A Roman military cohort or a detachment associated with one; the exact arrest-party size is uncertain.
A charcoal fire, linking Peter's denial in chapter 18 with restoration in chapter 21.
From or out of; Jesus says his kingdom is not sourced from this world.
